title: p99-p95-tail-latency-deep-dive with Skyward Systems
summary: Deep technical session focused on p95/p99 tail latency for streaming and non-streaming generation. Discussed KV cache warmup, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, network hops (VPC peering vs public), and on-prem constraints. Agreed to run end-to-end benchmark with customer traces and share patch-level perf notes.
next_steps: Redwood to run E2E benchmark using Skyward trace (shared script) and post results - due 2027-11-10
Send security docs (SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration notes) - Maya to send by 2027-11-04
Schedule follow-up canary run with Dedicated config - target week of 11/15
action_items: Samir Patel: prepare benchmark harness and run on Redwood dedicated pool using customer's trace | due: 2027-11-10
Maya Ortiz: share SOC2 pack and KMS integration runbook | due: 2027-11-04
Priya Rao / Ethan Chen: provide representative production traces and SLOs | due: 2027-11-05
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Maya (CSM), Priya (Skyward CTO), Ethan (Infra), Lena (ML Eng), Tom (SRE), Nora (Security)

[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick agenda: p95/p99 deep dive, streaming vs non-streaming, kv cache warmup, batching and quantization tradeoffs and then next steps.
[00:23] Priya: thanks Alex. we mostly care because our product has tight interactive SLOs for the operator console — 200ms median, p95 350ms, p99 700ms right now and the p99 spikiness is killing UX.
[00:40] Samir (SE): got it. can you remind us of your current stack — are you on public cloud endpoints or self-hosted?
[00:47] Ethan: we run in our VPC on GCP; inference is a mix, some hosted endpoints via third-party but majority is in our own k8s clusters. we have gRPC frontends, and the network path hits a couple of hops — internal LB, service mesh, then GPU node.
[01:08] Samir: cool. two immediate things that drive tail: KV cache warmup and network hop variance. for long-context streaming calls the KV cache and attention recompute can add jitter if the cache isn't hot. also small-batch workloads are sensitive to kernel latency.
[01:30] Lena (ML Eng): can you explain how your KV cache works again? we sometimes call it "K-V cash" in our notes so forgive the typo.
[01:36] Samir: yeah no worries. Redwood's runtime maintains per-request KV cache for autoregressive generation; for streaming we keep the cache pinned in GPU memory across chunks which keeps recompute low. cold requests or new sessions cause re-population and lead to higher p99. we also do prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[02:05] Tom (SRE): our big problem is bursty traffic, short-lived sessions where each session is like 8-12 tokens and many first-time users so cache hit rate is low.
[02:18] Samir: that explains it. in those cases batching isn't straightforward because latency SLOs are tight. we often recommend small-window batching (5-20ms gather) and partial streaming where you stream but allow a short micro-batch to amortize kernel overhead.
[02:40] Priya: small-window batching — does that increase p50 but help p99? what's the tradeoff?
[02:48] Samir: it can slightly increase median by the window delay (e.g., 5-10ms) but reduces tail by amortizing fixed kernel costs and reducing per-request kernel launch variance. we've seen 20-40% p99 improvement in similar workloads by tuning gather window plus prefix KV reuse.
[03:12] Nora (Security): curious about on-prem / VPC implications — if we run in our VPC with private peering, are there additional network hops that add tail?
[03:21] Alex: yes, public endpoints often have fewer network hops if direct peering exists, but private deployments add VPC routing, NAT and sometimes VPN/SD-WAN which increases variance. we recommend colocating the inference pool in the same subnet as the service mesh or using an ENI/placement group to reduce cross-AZ hops.
[03:48] Ethan: our trace shows occasional 200-400ms spikes that correlate with cross-az traffic. would moving to dedicated in-region capacity help?
[03:56] Samir: absolutely — dedicated capacity reduces host-level scheduling variance; it also gives you control to pin GPUs and take advantage of huge page warmups. it won't eliminate KV cold starts though.
[04:12] Alex: quick demo note — streaming vs non-streaming: streaming sends partial tokens as they generate which helps perceived latency, but in our runtime there is still a tradeoff — streaming increases per-chunk overhead and can widen p99 if the chunking is too small.
[04:34] Lena: can you quantify? our p99 currently is 700ms — what's realistic after optimizations?
[04:40] Samir: with careful batching, prefix caching and dedicated nodes, we've seen p95 drop to ~250-300ms and p99 to ~450-500ms for similar 1-2k token context workloads, assuming network hops are controlled. with quantization (int8) you can shave additional 20-30% in kernel time but may affect quality in edge cases.
[05:05] Priya: about quantization — we tried an aggressive int8 profile and saw some hallucination increase. what's your recommended approach?
[05:12] Samir: recommended path is fp16 baseline, then ptq/int8 on non-critical models or with per-layer calibration. Redwood supports mixed-precision profiles — you can run a pilot with eval prompts to measure regressions. we also have a fallback policy to run critical requests on fp16 if quality fails thresholds.
[05:40] Ethan: network-wise, we use a private peering to our cloud infra but there is a firewall box and an outbound NAT. any suggestions to reduce tail from those hops?
[05:50] Alex: remove extra NATs, avoid cross-AZ hops by placing inference in same AZ, use direct ENI attachment or private link. also use keepalives and connection pooling to avoid TLS handshake spikes.
[06:10] Tom: what about grpc vs http? we are on gRPC.
[06:14] Samir: gRPC is fine; make sure you use long-lived streams and HTTP/2 multiplexing to avoid per-request TLS churn. For streaming consider sending fewer, larger chunks rather than many tiny ones.
[06:28] Priya: latency budgets: median 200ms, p95 350ms, p99 below 500ms ideally. is that feasible?
[06:36] Samir: yes with dedicated capacity, small-window batching, prefix caching, and network path simplification. run the E2E benchmark and we'll baseline.
[06:46] Lena: curious about kernel-level jitter — do GPUs sometimes have thermal throttling or scheduling that effects p99?
[06:52] Samir: yes, on multi-tenant GPUs or when there's host contention you'll see variance. Dedicated nodes avoid that. also small kernel launches for attention ops are sensitive to launch overhead; fused kernels and JIT caching helps reduce that.
[07:12] Priya: can you walk through what you plan to run for the benchmark?
[07:16] Samir: we'll take your trace, replay at production QPS, measure streaming vs non-streaming with our batching heuristic, run with fp16 and int8 profiles, and record p50/p95/p99 and memory/kv hit rates. we'll also run cross-AZ vs same-AZ to quantify network tail.
[07:34] Ethan: will you need any agents on our side?
[07:37] Samir: just the trace and an SSH key if we need to run a light probe in your VPC; otherwise we can simulate the network characteristics if you prefer to keep things closed.
[07:48] Nora: security question — how do you handle KMS and keys for private deployments?
[07:53] Alex: we integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM, we don't store plaintext keys in Redwood control plane for private deployments, and we provide audit logs for all key operations. Maya will send the SOC2 + KMS integration notes after the call.
[08:06] Priya: good. one more thing — our model is a custom 13B, has large KV size. any specific tuning?
[08:14] Samir: for 13B models, KV size and cache eviction policies matter. increase GPU memory headroom, enable selective KV eviction for long sequences, and consider prefix deduplication. quantization helps reduce KV footprint too.
[08:34] Tom: we also saw a weird case where a single slow disk IO on a logging process added 150ms to some requests. how often do you see infra issues outside of model execution?
[08:44] Samir: sometimes. that's why tail debugging pairs tracing (span-level) with token-level timing. Redwood's console shows per-request token timing and host-level metrics to correlate IO spikes.
[09:02] Priya: ok let's recap the plan.
[09:06] Alex: recap: Redwood runs E2E benchmark with Skyward traces (Samir), compare streaming vs non-streaming, run fp16 and int8, run same-AZ and cross-AZ scenarios, and share a write-up plus optimized batching suggestions. Maya sends security docs. follow-up canary for dedicated in mid-November.
[09:30] Priya: sounds good. thanks all.

(Transcript continues with some Q&A and side chatter omitted for brevity)

[60:05] Alex: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the benchmark link and share the results.
[60:12] Priya: thanks — look forward to it.
